newsitem.title: USA: Court orders $3 million payment for insider trading.
newsitem.headline: Court orders $3 million payment for insider trading.

text.p: A federal judge Thursday ordered Thomas Warde, one of seven prominent figures in a landmark insider trading case, to pay more than $3 million in penalties, interest and alleged illegal trading profits.

Warde, a former officer of Manhattan Capital Corp., a Los Angeles investment group, was named in the Securities and Exchange Commission's 1992 civil suit as part of the group dubbed the Society Seven for its connections to New York's social elite.

A jury in January of this year returned a verdict siding with the SEC's charges against Warde. "We think it's appropriate that the Jury found Warde liable based on the evidence and appropriate that the Jury's verdict was upheld," said Barry Rashkover, senior trial counsel for the SEC's Northeast regional office.

Rashkover said the latest action closes the door on the agency's civil case, in which it alleged the socialites made a total of at least $13 million from trading on confidential information between 1987 and 1989 about Kidde Inc.'s pending merger.

"Warde made repeated trades in Kidde warrants, delayed the SEC's investigation by asserting the Fifth Amendment and gave conflicting testimony throughout the course of the litigation to cover up his fraud," wrote Manhattan Federal Judge Shira Scheindlin in an opinion and order.

The SEC in its 1992 case alleged the wealthy men started the $13 million scheme less than a year after the government brought its much-touted 1986 securities fraud actions against powerful stock speculator Ivan Boesky and other prominent Wall Street figures.
In the latest development, Warde was issued a permanent injunction and ordered to turn over $871,725 of alleged illegal profits, $1,264,501 in interest and to pay a $871,725 penalty.
The SEC had sought a penalty equalling three times the amount of Warde's ill-gotten gains, but the judge reduced the penalty to the amount of the profits.

"While I find that Warde's conduct justifed the imposition of a civil penalty, I do not find that the 300 percent penalty requested by the SEC is warranted," the judge wrote, adding that Warde did not try to conceal his trades nor did he have a prior history of insider trading violations.
Warde's attorney could not be reached for comment.
The SEC at trial contended Warde received his tips from his friend Edward Downe Jr., the son-in-law of Henry Ford II and a former director of both Bear Stearns Cos Inc. and Kidde.
In 1994, Downe settled the SEC's charges and agreed to pay more than $11 million. He also pleaded guilty to related criminal charges in 1993.
Kidde later merged into Hanson Industries, the U.S. arm of Hanson Trust Plc.
